B04_00: Every aerobic cell relies on this defence to keep the oxidative by-products of respiration from damaging its membranes, proteins and genetic material, while also shaping redox-dependent signalling. It operates inside the cell, in mitochondria and in the extracellular space. Its failure contributes to oxidative stress in neurodegenerative disease, chronic inflammation and ageing, and immune cells that deliberately produce oxidants depend on the same balance.
B04_01: Cells throughout the body mount this cytoprotective response when faced with oxidative stress, low oxygen, heavy metal exposure, inflammation or the breakdown of red blood cells, limiting tissue injury. It is especially important in blood vessels, liver, spleen and the macrophages that handle released blood pigment. People who lack this activity develop a rare syndrome of haemolysis, endothelial damage and severe inflammation.
B04_02: Cells exposed to sustained oxidative damage, for example after oncogene activation or prolonged exposure to antiviral cytokines, enter a permanent growth arrest rather than continuing to divide. This acts as a tumour-suppressive barrier that stops damaged cells from propagating. The cost is a gradual build-up of senescent cells in ageing tissues, which contributes to age-related decline in tissue function.
B04_03: Cells facing oxidant or electrophilic challenge redirect their sugar metabolism to build up reducing power and nucleotide precursors, improving their survival under stress. In normal tissues this protects against chemical and oxidative injury. Tumours with permanently switched-on stress defences exploit the same programme to fuel rapid proliferation and to resist chemotherapy and radiation, making it relevant to cancer treatment failure.
B04_04: Cells across the body must decide when to launch a protective response to heat, oxidative insult and protein-damaging stress, and when to stop it. Getting this timing right matters for health: chronic activation helps tumour cells cope with their heavy load of abnormal proteins, whereas a blunted response leaves neurons vulnerable to the protein aggregates seen in neurodegenerative disease.
B04_05: Secretory cells that make large quantities of protein, such as antibody-producing plasma cells, hormone-secreting pancreatic beta cells and matrix-depositing connective tissue cells, depend on this adaptive stress response to expand their secretory capacity. When it fails these cells cannot sustain secretion and tend to die. Loss of one of its targets causes Wolfram syndrome, a disorder of juvenile diabetes and neurodegeneration.
B04_06: Cells that have permanently stopped dividing after DNA damage or oncogene activation keep signalling to their surroundings through secreted inflammatory factors. In the short term this reinforces their arrest and attracts immune cells that clear damaged cells. When it persists, it fuels chronic inflammation, tissue ageing, loss of epithelial character and growth of neighbouring premalignant cells, linking senescence to age-related disease and cancer.
B04_07: After cells recover from heat or other protein-damaging stress, their protective response has to be wound down once folding capacity again matches demand. Shutting it off too late is costly and helps tumour cells become addicted to stress protection, while shutting it off too early leaves damaged proteins unresolved, with consequences for cell survival in stressed tissues.
B04_08: Professional secretory cells such as antibody-producing plasma cells, liver cells and pancreatic beta cells rely on this arm of the endoplasmic reticulum stress response to enlarge their folding capacity and survive heavy protein loads. When it fails, chronic stress pushes these cells toward death, a process implicated in diabetes and liver disease and in the decision of stressed cells to live or die.
B04_09: Cells that acquire a strong cancer-driving mutation often respond by permanently stopping division instead of proliferating. This arrest, seen in benign moles and early premalignant lesions, is one of the body's first barriers to tumour formation. When it fails, a single initiating mutation can expand into a growing lesion, so escaping this barrier is a key step in cancer progression.
B04_10: The overall capacity of a cell to defend itself against oxidants and toxic chemicals depends on how strongly its master stress-defence programme is expressed. Tumours that boost it become resistant to oxidative stress and chemotherapy, whereas tissues with too little are vulnerable to oxidative and chemical injury. This control ties stress resistance to proliferative, inflammatory and developmental signals in growing and inflamed tissues.
B04_11: Cells under oxidative or chemical stress reshape their central energy metabolism to supply reducing power and the building blocks for membranes and DNA. In normal tissues this helps them survive toxic insults. In tumours whose stress-defence programme is permanently switched on, the same rewiring supports rapid anabolic growth and resistance to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, where redox balance and proliferation meet.
B04_12: Tissues with heavy secretory demands use this family of membrane-anchored regulators to expand their protein-export capacity. Individual members serve particular tissues: bone-forming osteoblasts that secrete bone matrix, cartilage-forming cells, and liver cells controlling fat handling and the acute-phase response to inflammation. Loss of the osteoblast member causes a form of osteogenesis imperfecta, the brittle bone disease, showing its importance for skeletal formation.
B04_13: Beyond protecting cells from oxidants, the cellular stress-defence programme shapes inflammatory responses, linking a cell's redox state to immune signalling and the recruitment of monocytes. Its effects are context-dependent, sometimes promoting and sometimes restraining inflammation. Loss of this control contributes to chronic inflammatory and oxidative-stress-associated disease, including airway and vascular inflammation, which is why drugs that activate it are pursued as anti-inflammatory agents.
B04_14: When protein folding is overwhelmed in the secretory compartment, cells launch a stress programme that either restores balance or commits them to death, and it also responds to nutrient shortage. Chronic activation of this programme contributes to the loss of secretory cells such as pancreatic beta cells in diabetes and of neurons in neurodegenerative disease, and it shapes local inflammatory signalling in stressed tissues.
B04_15: In normal tissues the cellular stress-defence programme helps cells expel toxic foreign chemicals, contributing to protection against environmental toxins. In tumours where this programme is permanently switched on, the same capacity lets cancer cells pump out chemotherapy drugs and survive treatment, as in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer. A mechanism that is protective in healthy tissue thus becomes a major liability in treated cancer.
B04_16: How quickly cells dispose of their master stress-defence regulator determines how well they cope with oxidative and chemical stress. This disposal route connects the stress response to growth factor and hormonal signals, so that growth-stimulated cells raise their defences. Its loss in tumours contributes to constant activation of stress defences, which helps cancer cells resist chemotherapy.
B04_17: Secretory cells experiencing a build-up of misfolded proteins rely on this stress pathway to decide how much extra folding and quality-control capacity to build. This member is a weak, moderating component that dampens rather than amplifies the response, helping to tune how much secretory capacity a stressed cell builds and preventing excessive reactions in tissues with fluctuating protein-export demands.
B04_18: Present in most tissues, this repressor sets the threshold at which cells activate their oxidative stress defences and handle breakdown of blood pigment. Its abundance influences redox balance and red blood cell and immune gene programmes. In disease it affects new blood vessel formation after ischaemic injury and the metastatic spread of breast cancer cells, making its control relevant to vascular and cancer biology.
B04_19: Cells facing low oxygen, amino acid shortage or an accumulation of misfolded proteins need an adaptive stress response to survive, and the oxidative stress-defence programme feeds into it. Under sustained stress the same response can tip cells toward death. Tumour cells, including non-small cell lung cancer, depend on this link for stress tolerance and for making the amino acids they need to grow.
B04_20: Cells exposed to heat, oxidants and other protein-damaging insults rely on the heat shock response to survive; without it misfolded proteins accumulate unchecked and cells die under stress. Constitutive activation supports the stress tolerance of tumour cells, which makes this response a target in cancer therapy, while its decline is linked to protein-aggregation disorders and ageing.
B04_21: This antioxidant response allows cells throughout the body to survive oxidative stress and exposure to toxic foreign chemicals, including drugs and environmental pollutants. Its loss sensitises tissues to inflammation, chemical injury and degeneration. In tumours its constitutive activation protects cancer cells and confers drug resistance, and it is coupled to the cell's wider integrated response to stress.
B04_22: Cells that have suffered irreparable genetic damage or have exhausted their replicative lifespan stop dividing for good, and a large-scale reorganisation of their nuclei makes this exit permanent. This locked-in arrest underlies the tumour-suppressive effect of senescence, preventing damaged cells from proliferating. It also contributes to the altered nuclear architecture seen in cells of aged tissues.
B04_23: When the cellular stress-defence programme is permanently switched on, as in many aggressive lung and other epithelial cancers, it shifts from protecting normal tissue to promoting tumour growth. In this setting it supports cancer cell survival, independence from external growth signals and resistance to chemotherapy and radiation. Its activation marks aggressive disease, turning a defence system into a driver of tumour progression.
